utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you compared these reports from the media, were you able to conclude what was the truth? Was it possible at all to determine what the truth was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It was impossible for me to determine what the truth was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any type of information that you received from direct participants in any of these events?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, throughout this period -- we are now entering 1992, up until the beginning of the war with the Muslims -- at any time feel threatened by the Muslims, that is, by your Muslim neighbours in particular?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: My Muslim neighbours? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: There were frequent threats, that is to say, we were threatened when we heard the term "Mujahedin." That was the frightening word.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In what sense were you afraid when you heard the term "Mujahedin"? Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, they were some foreign mercenaries from some Arab countries who had come to fight for Islam for the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they existed in Zenica, and Zenica was the bordering municipality, if you look at Zenica, Vitez and Ahmici and Pirici, where I come from, so that was the nearest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So people spoke about them as warriors to propagate religion. But were they also talked about as to their conduct, whether they adhered to the rules of warfare or the prevalent rules with regard to their behaviour toward civilians, or were they also spoken of as something quite separate and different?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, the tales told were that these people would slaughter others and that they would storm the village and so on. There were terrible stories going about, and you could believe them or not believe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But whether it's true or not, you had your doubts, and this idea was implanted in your mind.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, the Muslims would frighten you by referring to the Mujahedins. Did you frighten the Muslims in any way? Not you personally but I mean generally.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, I learned some things from Senad Topoljak who worked with me and lived in the town, and he said that -- I don't know what period this was, whether it was the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993 -- that in Vitez, there were some people from Herzegovina, there was an army of Herzegovinian men, and their behaviour was provocative, they would shoot above their heads in cafes, they would take drinks and not pay for them, they were generally carousing and so on, and I saw this on several occasions myself, people going through the town with weapons, drunk and rowdy, and I gained the impression that Senad was afraid of them. Well, I was afraid too, not only him. So that this fear did exist and it was tangible, you could feel the fear from this army, and it was a sort of Herzegovina army, men from Herzegovina, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, at that particular time, from the summer of 1992 up until the beginning of the war, was there any violence in town? For example, would they break somebody's cafe, demolish it, shoot at somebody's windows, throw in a bomb or something like that, in the town of Vitez, I'm asking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is in line with what I said a moment ago, that there were rumours and people said that this was done by the people from Herzegovina, that cafes were blown up, that they shot into the air at random, and that their behaviour was generally rowdy and that they behaved badly, that he would have a long-barrelled weapon. This occurred at the end of 1992; I don't know if it was already 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But tell us, please, in your own village where you lived, was there any behaviour of that kind there, any violence towards the Muslims, whether there was random shooting, people from -- and towards the Muslim houses in what was considered to be Ahmici, or was nothing going on there with respect to violent behaviour?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time in Ahmici, there was nothing of that kind going on, but by the main road there was. From time to time, a car would go by, for example, and people would shoot out of it into the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But what about the main road? These were not locals.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No. People would come in by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about the villagers themselves.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, there was nothing of that kind amongst the villagers, the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have just heard of the kind of tensions that existed and the tensions in the media, that they always blamed the other side for anything that occurred. Would you now tell us something about the village guards or village watch. What were the village guards? We've been talking a lot about them. Well, let's hear what they were because we heard yesterday, the BBC film we saw, that the Muslims, via the village guards, protected their houses. Could you tell us what is meant by the village guards in your particular village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when I watched the film, I think his name was Nurija, shown on the film, and I thought poor old Nurija, the situation was similar where we were with just some little differences. But that was it more or less. As far as the village guards were concerned or village watch, I know that at Zume they started forming these village guards and it was the winter of 1992, but in Ahmici, the Muslim neighbours, during that particular period, we Kupreskics did not have watches of that kind until February or March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, among the Kupreskic houses, how many of you, how many men were there who were capable of doing shifts within this village guard? We're not going to stick to the 65 age limit as existed in the army. But how many of you were able to go out at night carrying a gun and take part in this village guard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Three of us. I myself, Ivica, and Mirjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And that's all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the Kupreskic houses, that was all. And as that was so, then we wanted to have the Sakics, Samija, and the ones who were nearer, the Pudzine houses' people to join us, so there were not only three of us, there were 10 or 12 people in all, counting them, because the three of us couldn't hold any village watch of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us how you started doing these guard shifts? I interrupted you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the village guards were at Zume. The Muslims stood guard, our neighbours, in the village. And in February or March, somewhere thereabouts, we too stood guard several times, on several occasions, but we began to do this in a more serious fashion in April, after the JNA shelling of the SPS in Vitez, the company there, and the town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So how did it come about that village guards were formed at all? Was there an initiative from outside? Did this initiative come from outside? Did they ask you to set up village guards in the village, or did this come about in some other way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, the initiative came from the village itself. I remember that my father said to me, "Well, look here. These people, our neighbours, are holding village guards at Zume. They're all awake whereas you're all sleeping. They go to work and you sleep at night." And Dragan Vidovic's father told him the same thing and so did Mirko Sakic's father. They all said this. And I remember on one occasion, Dragan and I, when I took part in the village watch with Dragan Vidovic for the first time and I did my shift, that might have been in March perhaps, I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't tell me how it came about that you went to do your guard shift for the first time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, I went there for the first time with Dragan, as I said. He called me. He said that he was at Sakics' place, I don't know which one, but he went visiting, he went to have a cup of coffee, went to the Sakics' place, and the two of them had agreed that this Sakic would see, with those down there, whether they wanted to, and that Dragan would contact us to see whether we were in favour of this, and when Dragan told me, I said, "Well, yes," I wasn't against because I could see that there were village guards set up all over the place. So a few days later, he came and said that the two of us were to do our shift for a certain amount of time. So that is my first recollection of when I did my shift within this village guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How often did you have to do this village guard duty -- once a month, twice a month? -- when you had already started this? How often?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us say up until the 20th of October, tell us that first, and then from the 20th of October to the 16th of April, tell us about that next.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: So in those first few days, only a few of us wanted to do this village guard duty. Some people didn't want to. Later on, when there were about ten of us, then we would do two-hour shifts per night, so we had five to our shifts to cover the entire night. So we would go out, all of us, every night and do our two-hour shift. If I did my shift from, say, 1.00 to 3.00 a.m., the next evening -- we had this automatic system where I would do from 3.00 to 5.00 a.m. So that I would have all the shifts, the first, the middle shift, and the last shift, and everybody liked to do the last shift or the first shift so you could do your shift and then go home and have a sleep. So that we were out every night. If we wanted to do regular village guard duty, we would all have to be there and do two-hour shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What would happen if somebody could not go out for his shift, that is to say, up to this 20th of October period? For example, if someone went down with the flu?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, things like that did happen. They would stay at home and sleep and the other people would carry on. Quite simply, that shift would not be carried out. Sometimes somebody would replace them, but not always. So it wasn't very serious, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have completed this general section relating to the village guards. We will now go on to speak about whether he distributed the shifts. But if you agree, we could perhaps take a break there and adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now until tomorrow. Before adjourning, let me ask Counsel Puliselic a question. I would like Counsel Puliselic to inquire about the health of Mr. Dragan Papic. Is he in hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes, he went to hospital today, and as far as I have been informed, the operation has been scheduled for tomorrow. That is all I know. I know nothing more than that. So tomorrow or the day after, we will receive further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. All right. So we adjourn now. Tomorrow we will start at 10.00, because at 9.00, as you know, the Tadic judgement will be delivered. From 10.00 to 1.00. All right. We adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of July, 1999, at 10.00 a.m.
